thread.title: Dow Rises 241 Points Because Strong Earnings Never Lie

title: Dow Rises 241 Points Because Strong Earnings Never Lie
text:
Dow Rises 241 Points Because Strong Earnings Never Lie By Oct. 31, 2018 5:19 p.m. ET Order Reprints Michael Haddad Text size
Trick or Treat. After a painful month, stocks ended the month on a sweet note Wednesday, helped by a host of upbeat earnings reports. In today’s After the Bell , we… …breath a sigh of relief; …review the month that was; and …cheer Molson Coors Brewing ’s (TAP) results.
Creepy and Kooky
Monsters and ghouls come out on Halloween, but after living through this October it’ll take more than a cheap costume to scare investors. Still, there was more treat than trick today, as stocks closed with gains for two consecutive days for the first and the final time for October, helped by earnings reports from Facebook (FB) and General Motors (GM).
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 241.12 points, or 0.97%, to 25,115.76 while the S&P 500 rose 29.11 points, or 1.09%, to 2711.74, and the Nasdaq Composite climbed 144.25 points, or 2.01%, to 7305.90. For the former two, it was the best two-day streak since February. However for the month, The Dow fell 5.1%, while the S&P 500 slumped 6.9%, and the Nasdaq tumbled 9.2%.
For nervous investors there was no shortage of frights in October. Hopes for a quick resolution to the trade war with China are fading, the Federal Reserve appears committed to its interest-rate hike regime with bears eyeing up a potential inversion of the yield curve (a previous harbinger of recession), one-time darlings like tech are selling off as markets shift away from risk, polarization and violence has been rampant ahead of midterm elections, and we’re approaching the one-year anniversary of corporate tax cuts, which will remove a year-over-year profit tailwind as U.S. and global growth is expected to ease.
When you put it all together, maybe we should be grateful stocks had any gains at all. But of course, there’s not only bad news out there. “Even though the list of worries has grown in October, it is quite reassuring to know that consensus estimates for 2019 S&P 500 earnings per share actually increased this month!” writes LPL Financial’s Ryan Detrick. “Call us old school, but we still think earnings drive long-term stock gains, and this is a great sign amid all the market volatility.”
Certainly fundamentals have provided a floor amid mounting worries. While gross domestic product is unlikely to remain as robust as last quarter’s 3.5% reading, the U.S. economy remains on strong footing, consumer confidence remains high, and unemployment has reached decade lows without too much corresponding inflation.
Thus, Piper Jaffray’s Craig Johnson argues that recent selloffs don’t represent “the start of a bear market” but rather a “correction within a bull market at this juncture.” He believes we’ll see a bottom emerge in the coming weeks, but that investors may want to exercise patience, waiting for more “evidence of a capitulation and/or for support to be established.” Yet he reiterated his S&P 500 year-end target of 2,850.
Patience is a virtue, and Johnson isn’t the only one stumping for it. Massud Ghaussy, senior analyst at Nasdaq, believes investors should “expect continued turbulence as risk is being repriced.” He warns that tariffs will not provide any support to markets, but that trade should be offset by “strong tailwinds” like ongoing economic growth.
Still, waiting is easier if there’s reason for hope. To that end, after today’s sugar rush, a strong report from Apple (AAPL) Thursday could be just the palate cleanser the market needs for a better November. At least we hope so .
The Hot Stock
Molson Coors bubbled to the top of the index, following its third-quarter earnings report.
Molson Coors gained $5.79, or 10%, to $64, a stark contrast to Anheuser-Busch InBev ’s (BUD) post-earnings selloff .
The alcoholic beverage maker earned $1.84 a share on revenue of $2.93 billion. Analysts were looking for EPS of $1.59 on revenue of $2.92 billion.
Cowen & Co.’s Vivien Azer reiterated a Market Perform rating on the stock, writing that while the report “was a welcome improvement after a tough first half of the year, U.S. beer challenges continue to persist and Molson Coors will need to address pressure in Coors Light over the remainder of the year and into 2019.”
Year to date, Molson Coors is down 22%.
The Biggest Loser
Baxter International (BAX) slid to the bottom of the index, after offering downbeat guidance.
Baxter lost $6.15, or 9% to $62.51.
The medical-device maker said it earned 80 cents a share on revenue of $2.77 billion. Analysts were expecting EPS of 74 cents on revenue of $2.79 billion. However, for the fourth quarter, Baxter said it sees EPS of 71 cents to 73 cents, compared with the 77 cent consensus estimate.
Edward Jones’ John Boylan reiterated a Hold rating on Baxter shares. He writes that the quarter included several issues that likely spooked investors, including changing demand patterns and distributor destocking for its Clinical Nutrition and Medication Delivery businesses in the wake of the Puerto Rican hurricane last year (Baxter facilities on the island were damaged) and lighter-than-expected sales for its renal business. “Positively, we feel Baxter is doing an admirable job controlling its costs and increasing its profitability.”
Year to date, Baxter is down 3.3%.
